lines.text: Every sport has its own specialised equipment, and knowing this vocabulary is essential for discussing fitness, following commentary, and participating in activities in English-speaking countries. Football (soccer) requires boots (cleats in American English), shin pads, a ball, goalposts, and a pitch (field). Cricket uses a bat, ball, stumps, pads, gloves, and a helmet. Tennis demands a racket (not 'racquet' in modern usage), balls, a net, and appropriate court shoes. Rugby needs a ball, mouthguard, headguard, and studded boots. Swimming involves a swimsuit, goggles, a swimming cap, and kickboard. Athletics (track and field) uses starting blocks, hurdles, javelins, discuses, shot puts, and relay batons. Cycling requires a bicycle (or bike), helmet, padded shorts, cleats, and a pump. Boxing equipment includes gloves, a mouthguard, headgear, a punch bag, and a ring. Gym and fitness vocabulary covers dumbbells, barbells, kettlebells, resistance bands, yoga mats, exercise balls, and treadmills. Protective gear is important across sports: helmets, pads, guards, visors, and goggles protect players from injury. British and American terminology often differs: 'kit' (British) versus 'gear' or 'uniform' (American), 'trainers' versus 'sneakers', 'pitch' versus 'field'. Understanding these terms allows learners to follow sports conversations, shop for equipment, and participate fully in the sporting culture of English-speaking countries.

lines.text: In British English, 'kit' refers to sports clothing and equipment collectively: 'football kit', 'PE kit', 'gym kit'. Americans use 'gear' or 'uniform'. 'Kit' also means the branded shirt: 'The new Arsenal kit looks great.' This is a common cultural vocabulary difference.

lines.text: In Britain, football boots are a cultural icon. Children debate which brand is best, and professional players' boot choices make news. 'Boot room' was famously part of Liverpool FC's culture — where coaches gathered and strategies were discussed.

lines.text: Cricket equipment has changed little in centuries: the 'willow' bat (made from willow wood), the red leather ball (white for limited-overs), and the distinctive pads and gloves. 'Getting your bat' means being selected to play — equipment as metaphor.

lines.text: Gym vocabulary has exploded: 'reps' (repetitions), 'sets', 'HIIT' (High-Intensity Interval Training), 'gains', 'PB' (personal best), 'spotter' (person who assists). This vocabulary crosses into motivation language: 'no pain, no gain', 'push through the wall'.
